## Introduction

At the core of the foosball3 package lies the database. It is an
[SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) relational database meant to store
foosball tournaments and its results.

You can create a virtually blank database with `foosball3_create_db()`,
but you can also import existing data using `foosball3_import_db()`.
The latter let's you import data from previously exported foosball data.
This can be an SQLite database file, or a zip-archive containing all
required data tables (as CSV files).

This import function will create a copy of the database at the designated
location, and will attempt to fix changes in database structure introduced
since the database was last stored.

Let's import the example data provided with the package, such that we can
have a closer look at how the data is organised.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(foosball3)
library(dplyr)
library(RSQLite)
example_file <- system.file(package = "foosball3", "example.zip")
target_file  <- tempfile(fileext = ".db")
foosball3_import_db(example_file, target_file)
```

## Database Structure

In order to work with the database, we need to open a connection to it:

```{r connection}
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), target_file)
```

If you have both `dm` and `DiagrammeRsvg` installed, you will see a visualisation
of the database relations below.

```{r structure, include={requireNamespace("dm") && requireNamespace("DiagrammeRsvg")}, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
foosball3_get_schema(con, FALSE) |>
  dm::dm_draw() |>
  DiagrammeRsvg::export_svg() |>
  ## strip DOCTYPE from svg code
  stringr::str_replace("(?s).*?(?=<svg)", "") |>
  cat()
```

From this scheme, a few important tables will be highlighted.

### Tournaments

At the center of all tables is the table named 'tournaments'. It contains
a list of tournaments and some essential information about it, such as:

  * Where is it held?
  * When was it held?
  * What kind of tournament is it?

```{r tournaments}
tbl(con, "tournaments") |> collect()
```

Technically, the database structure is capable of handling different
types of tournament structures, but the graphical user interface
([`foosball3()`]), currently only implements one type.
<!-- a vignette on tournament structure(s) should be written,
and a link inserted here -->

### People

Another important table is the table named 'persons'. It contains a list
of people and their name. This list is used to enroll participants in
tournament or assign then as tournament organisers. Note that a single
individual can join multiple tournaments. For each tournament, a person
is given a unique participant id. This means that a single person can
have multiple participant ids.

```{r persons}
tbl(con, "persons") |> collect()
```

> ## Disclaimer
> Note that the example data is based on real tournament data. To protect
> participant's privacy, locations and names have been anonymised using
> Star Trek locations and characters.
> 
> Star Trek and all associated names are trademarks of CBS/Paramount. This
> open-source package is purely for educational/utility purposes and is not

An advantage of this approach is that statistics of individuals can
be collected and these statistics can be used to balance players
skill levels in matches.

### Locations, Tables and Balls

The database records 'locations' (where tables are located, tournaments
are organised, and where players are based); as well as 'tables' (and
accompanying 'periods' describing when tables are where); and 'balls'
to specify which ball is used during a match. You can of course use
dummies if you don't want to record these kinds of detail.

### And Many More

As the diagram with all tables in the database show, there are many
more tables. You can get details on each of these tables using
[foosball3_meta_data()]. It will give a description for each table
(next to each `"CREATE"` `field_name`) and all columns in the table.

## Views

All tables discussed above are plain tables, containing raw data.
The advantage of having them in a database is that *views* of the
data can be created. They can be used to simplify database complexity,
don't require physical storage of data.

Not all views will be presented here, but some notable ones will be
addressed. For completeness all available views are listed here:

```{r views, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
paste(
  "* ",
  RSQLite::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';") |>
    pull("name") |> sort()) |> paste(collapse = "\n") |>
  cat()
```

You can use 'participant_match_results' to find results of a specific
participant in any match of any tournament:

```{r match_result}
tbl(con, "participant_match_results")
```

But you can also look for aggregated results. For instance, player
statistics are summarised in 'player_statistics':

```{r player_stats}
tbl(con, "player_statistics")
```

Have fun exploring the provided example database, or collect your own
tournament results.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(target_file, TRUE, TRUE)
```
